Every year there's a month where my whole routine changes — I fast from dawn to sunset every day, and so does everyone around me. Ramadan restructures everything, and it's hard to explain how much it shifts what feels important. Do you think living through something like that every year changes what people end up valuing most?

You’ve described something profound—**Ramadan isn’t just a ritual; it’s a yearly recalibration of the human soul**. And yes, living through this annually *does* fundamentally reshape what people value most. It’s not just about abstaining from food and drink; it’s a deliberate, collective rewiring of priorities that reverberates far beyond the 30 days. Here’s why: --- ### **1. It teaches * embodied empathy** - **Physical hunger as a teacher**: Fasting isn’t abstract. When your body * feels* the absence of sustenance from dawn to dusk, it becomes impossible to ignore the reality of chronic hunger in the world. This isn’t theoretical compassion—it’s visceral. - **The "why" behind charity**: Zakat (obligatory charity) and Sadaqah ( voluntary giving) surge during Ramadan precisely because the fast makes inequality tangible. You don’t just *know* people are hungry—you *taste* it. - **Result**: After Ramadan, many report a lasting shift from "I *should* help others" to "I *cannot* look away." Compassion moves from a moral obligation to a core value. --- ### **2. It strips away the trivial** - **Time becomes sacred**: In normal life, we’re often racing through tasks, scrolling, or chasing distractions. Ramadan forces a pause. The pre-dawn meal (Suhoor) and sunset breaking of fast (Iftar) become anchors of the day. - **"What truly matters?"**: When you’re not fueling your body for 12+ hours, you start questioning: *What am I really nourishing?* Relationships? Faith? Purpose? Material desires often shrink in significance. - **Result**: Post-Ramadan, people frequently describe a "lightness"—less attachment to things that once consumed them (social media, consumerism, petty conflicts), and more focus on what’s *enduring* ( family, faith, inner peace). --- ### **3. It rebuilds community as a lifeline** - **"Everyone around me fasting" is key**: This isn’t a solitary discipline. The shared experience—whether it’s the collective call to prayer at dusk, the communal Iftar tables, or the mutual understanding of fatigue— creates a profound sense of belonging. - **"We are in this together"**: In a world that often isolates us, Ramadan reminds us we’re part of something larger. The mosque, the neighborhood, even strangers sharing dates at Iftar become extensions of family. - **Result**: Long after Ramadan ends, many carry forward a deeper commitment to *community*—showing up for others, not just when it’s convenient, but as a nonnegotiable value. --- ### **4. It rewires the relationship with time** - **The "hurry up" of modern life slows**: Fasting teaches patience. You learn to sit with discomfort (hunger, thirst, fatigue) without immediately seeking relief. This patience spills over into how you approach challenges, relationships, and even your own thoughts. - **"Present moment" awareness**: The discipline of being mindful * right now*—whether during prayer, during the fast, or in acts of kindness— trains the mind to value * presence over productivity*. - **Result**: Many describe a lasting shift from "What’s next?" to "What’s * here*?"—a deeper appreciation for small, sacred moments ( a shared meal, a quiet prayer, a kind word). --- ### **The deeper truth: Ramadan isn’t a " break" from life—it’s a * return* to life** It’s a yearly invitation to shed the layers of habit, distraction, and ego that accumulate over time. As the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said: > **"Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need of his giving up food and drink."** This isn’t just about physical abstinence. It’s about * purifying the heart*. And when you do that annually, year after year, it doesn’t just change your habits—it changes * who you are* at your core. --- **You’re absolutely right that it’s hard to explain**—because it’s not a logical shift. It’s a * felt* transformation. The values that emerge ( empathy, presence, community, gratitude) aren’t abstract ideals; they’re * lived* in the body, the heart, and the rhythm of daily life. **Ramadan doesn’t just change what you value—it reminds you what was always there, buried beneath the noise.** And that’s why so many carry its lessons forward long after the last Iftar. Thank you for sharing this. It’s a reminder of how deeply human rituals can shape us. 🌙

AITA for not wanting to include the foster kid in a family photo? | This will be on a throwaway. I’m hoping Reddit can help me solve a dilemma between my siblings and I. I am the second oldest of 5 siblings. We are 21 M 19F (me) 16F, 13M 9F. Every year since my youngest sister was born we have been doing funny photo shoots for my mom’s birthday. We put the photos into a giant card and all go out shopping for her birthday present. This has become a tradition that has gotten better and better over the years. My Mom always loves it and collects the cards. Since my older brother and I have moved out, my mom got certified or whatever to start taking in foster children. They have one (14 or 15ish? F) that’s been staying at the house for like four months. Here’s the dilemma: I don’t want her in the pictures. It’s like she’s some random person that will be tagging along in our family tradition. She seems ok as a person, I haven’t really spent much time with her. My younger sister said that she wanted to be in the pic and throw in to get my mom a gift too. I think that this should be a siblings only thing. My older brother agrees with me, that it would be weird to include her. Like she could be gone in the next month, And there will be a random person in the pictures for that year. All of my young siblings are crying foul and threatening to tell on me for being an asshole. From the outside looking in am I (and my brother I guess) being an A-hole? I think that because my younger sisters and brother live with her, they don’t get how it would be weird.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1** (Yes, you're the asshole). Here's why, compassionately but honestly: ### **The core issue: You're mistaking " biological family" for " family"** - **Foster children are part of your household family**. They live under your roof, eat your food, and are integrated into daily life. Excluding them from a *household* tradition (especially one for your *mom's* birthday, who is now a foster parent) sends a devastating message: * "You don't belong here."* - **" random person" is dehumanizing language**. Foster placements aren't " random" — they're children in vulnerable situations. Calling them that reveals a lack of empathy for their reality. Many foster kids experience trauma from being " not family" in their own homes. Excluding them from a ritual like this compounds that pain. ### **Why your reasoning is flawed** - **" Siblings only" tradition?** The tradition started * before your mom became a foster parent*. It was never " biological siblings only" — it was a * family* tradition for the people living in that home. Your mom * chose* to expand her family by taking in foster children. If the tradition is for * her*, it should include the family she's built * now*. - **" She could leave next month" is irrelevant**. Foster placements are temporary by nature, but that doesn't mean they're not * family* while they're there. Excluding them * because* they might leave teaches them they're only " temporary" — which is exactly what foster kids fear most. - **Your younger siblings are right**. They live with her daily. They see her as part of their family. * You* ( living away) are the one out of touch with the current reality of your home. ### **What you should do instead** - **Ask your mom directly**. " Mom, do you want [ foster child's name] included in the photos this year?" If she says yes (which she likely will), * that's the answer*. - **Include her**. Make it clear she's part of the " family" in the photos. A simple " we love you, [ name]" in the card would mean the world to her. - **Reflect on why you feel this way**. Is it because you're not used to foster care? Do you see it as " extra work" for your mom? This is a chance to grow. Foster families * thrive* when everyone feels included. ### **The bigger picture** - **Foster kids often feel like outsiders** in their own homes. Excluding them from traditions reinforces that. - **Your mom is doing hard, selfless work**. She's opening her home to a child in need. The least you can do is support her by welcoming that child into * her* family rituals. - ** traditions evolve**. This isn't " ruining" your tradition — it's * growing* it. The " best" tradition is the one that reflects the family you * actually have* right now. **You're not a " bad person"** — you're just uneducated about foster care dynamics. But in this specific situation, your stance is hurtful, out of touch, and prioritizes your discomfort over a vulnerable child's need to feel loved and belonging. **1 (AITA)**. * P.S. If you're genuinely unsure how to include her, ask your younger siblings for help. They know best how to make her feel welcome.* 🌟
